'''Halina Rubinsztein-Dunlop''' ([[née]] '''Rubinsztein'''; born 1950) {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO|FAA}} is an Australian physicist. She is a professor of [[physics]] at the [[University of Queensland]] and an Officer of the [[Order of Australia]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Allen|first=Elizabeth|date=29 April 2000|title=Atom lady|url=https://global-factiva-com.ezproxy.library.uq.edu.au/redir/default.aspx?P=sa&an=coumai0020010805dw4t00mqu&cat=a&ep=ASE|journal=Courier Mail}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> She has led pioneering research in [[atom optics]], laser micro-manipulation using [[optical tweezers]], laser enhanced ionisation [[spectroscopy]], [[biophysics]] and [[Quantum Physics|quantum physics]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://equs.org/users/prof-halina-rubinsztein-dunlop|title=Prof. Halina Rubinsztein-Dunlop {{!}} ARC Centre of Excellence for Engineered Quantum Systems|website=equs.org|access-date=2018-03-06}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Halina Rubinsztein (later Rubinsztein-Dunlop) was born in Poland to a [[Jewish]] family.<ref name=jwa/><ref>(11 June 2018) [https://www.jwire.com.au/the-queens-birthday-awards-the-2018-jewish-honourees/ The Queen’s Birthday Awards – The 2018 Jewish honorees] ''J-Wire''. Retrieved on 27 April 2025</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://spie.org/membership/women-in-optics/women-in-optics-planner/2010-wio-planner/rubinsztein-dunlop-halina?SSO=1|title=Halina Rubinsztein-Dunlop - 2010 SPIE Women in Optics Planner|access-date=2018-03-06}}</ref> She emigrated to Sweden<ref name=":0" /> where she obtained her BSc and PhD degree from the [[University of Gothenburg]].<ref name=":2" /> Rubinsztein-Dunlop was encouraged to be curious about the world by her mother, also a physicist. In an interview for [[SPIE]], she credits her mother's guidance and enthusiasm for science: "she taught me to persist and to be inquisitive and to want to understand, and also - and I think this is what was important - she showed me that women can do it. It was infectious,"<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=http://spie.org/newsroom/laser-sharp_halina-rubinsztein-dunlop-?SSO=1|title=Laser Sharp|website=spie.org|access-date=2018-10-23}}</ref> She moved to Australia in 1989,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.eait.uq.edu.au/uq-remembers|title=UQ remembers Emeritus Professor Keith Bullock, Dr Robert Wensley, QC and Emeritus Professor Gordon Dunlop|work=The Faculty of Engineering, Architecture and Information Technology|access-date=2018-03-06|archive-date=3 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180203124319/https://www.eait.uq.edu.au/uq-remembers|url-status=dead}}</ref> shortly after her marriage to engineer Gordon Dunlop.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Rubinsztein-Dunlop completed her PhD titled ''Atomic-beam magnetic resonance investigations of refractory elements and metastable states of lead'' at the University of Gothenburg in 1978.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Rubinsztein, Halina|date=1978|title=Atomic-beam magnetic resonance investigations of refractory elements and metastable states of lead|url=https://gupea.ub.gu.se/handle/2077/13863|language=sv}}</ref> After moving to Australia in 1989, Rubinsztein-Dunlop joined the Department of Physics at the [[University of Queensland]] where she formed a research group studying laser physics. In 1995, she helped establish a Science in Action program that was used for outreach in educational programs for schools.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://physicsmuseum.uq.edu.au/history-physics-department-1998|title=History of Physics Department to 1998 - Physics Museum - The University of Queensland, Australia|website=physicsmuseum.uq.edu.au|language=en|access-date=2018-03-06}}</ref>

Rubinsztein-Dunlop was appointed Professor of Physics in 2000.<ref name=":0" /> She held the role of Head of the Department of Physics as well as the Head of the School of Mathematics and Physics at the [[University of Queensland]] from 2006 to 2013. She is the Director of the Quantum Science Laboratory and leads one of the scientific programs of the [[Australian Research Council]] Centre of Excellence for Engineered Quantum Systems. In 2011 she was a guest editor for the [[Journal of Optics (IOP Publishing journal)|Journal of Optics]] on a special issue about [[optical tweezers]], published by the [[Institute of Physics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://iopscience.iop.org/issue/2040-8986/13/4|title=Journal of Optics, Volume 13, Number 4, April 2011 - IOPscience|website=iopscience.iop.org|language=en|access-date=2018-08-09}}</ref>

In 2016 Rubinsztein-Dunlop was made Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]].<ref name=":1" /> She was appointed an Officer of the [[Order of Australia]] (AO) in the Queen's [[2018 Birthday Honours]] List for "distinguished service to laser physics and nano-optics as a researcher, mentor and academic, to the promotion of educational programs, and to women in science".<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org.au/news-and-events/news-and-media-releases/queens-birthday-honours-seven-academy-fellows|title=Queen's Birthday honours for seven Academy Fellows {{!}} Australian Academy of Science|website=www.science.org.au|access-date=2018-06-13}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://smp.uq.edu.au/article/2018/06/uq-laser-physicist-recognised-queen%E2%80%99s-birthday-honours|title=UQ laser physicist recognised in Queen's birthday honours|date=11 June 2018|work=School of Mathematics and Physics|access-date=2018-06-13|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/2002027|title=Australian Honours database: Rubinsztein-Dunlop, Halina|publisher=Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet|accessdate=4 July 2018}}</ref>

During the 2018 international scientific conference [[SPIE]], the Optical Trapping and Optical Micromanipulation XV programme held a special session honouring Halina Rubinsztein-Dunlop.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://spie.org/OPN/conferencedetails/optical-trapping-manipulation#session-21|title=Conference Detail for Optical Trapping and Optical Micromanipulation XV|website=spie.org|access-date=2018-07-31}}</ref>

An [[Australian Museum Eureka Prizes|Australian Museum Eureka Prize]] was awarded to the University of Queensland Optical Physics in Neuroscience team, consisting of Rubinsztein-Dunlop alongside Ethan Scott and Itia Favre-Bulle for their study of the brain and how it detects gravity and motion.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.uq.edu.au/news/article/2018/08/eureka-moment-leading-uq-researchers|title=Eureka moment for leading UQ researchers|work=UQ News|access-date=2018-10-23|language=en}}</ref> The full title of the award is the 2018 UNSW Eureka Prize for Excellence in Interdisciplinary Scientific Research.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://australianmuseum.net.au/2018-eureka-prizes-winners|title=2018 Eureka Prizes Winners - Australian Museum|website=australianmuseum.net.au|language=en|access-date=2018-10-23|archive-date=1 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180901044355/https://australianmuseum.net.au/2018-eureka-prizes-winners|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Research ==
Rubinsztein-Dunlop conducts research that harnesses the power of optics and lasers to explore quantum and biological phenomena. She has published over 200 works in journals and books<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.co.uk/citations?user=4_sqVfYAAAAJ&hl=en|title=Halina Rubinsztein-Dunlop - Google Scholar Citations|website=scholar.google.co.uk|access-date=2018-08-09}}</ref> and has also been featured on radio and television. Rubinsztein-Dunlop is considered an originator of laser enhanced ionisation spectroscopy.<ref name=":1" />

=== Quantum Optics ===
Although her PhD involved looking at the [[hyperfine structure]] of atoms, she notes that her research was "not [using] the tiniest of the tiniest...I never worked with quarks or gluons...". She was however, fascinated by being able to interrogate nature at small level using light.<ref name=":6" /> Her team successfully demonstrated dynamical tunnelling in a [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose Einstein Condensate]] (BEC) using a modulated [[standing wave]].<ref name=":1" /> Rubinzstein-Dunlop's team has also observed dynamical tunnelling in quantum chaotic systems.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://equs.org/aol|title=The Bose-Einstein Condensate Laboratory {{!}} ARC Centre of Excellence for Engineered Quantum Systems|website=equs.org|access-date=2018-03-08}}</ref> In 2016, Rubinsztein-Dunlop, along with Tyler Neely and Guillaume Gauthier, imprinted images of [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] and Indian physicist [[Satyendra Nath Bose]] on a super-cold microscopic fluid, demonstrating a physics state predicted by Einstein and Bose in 1925 but first achieved in 1995.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.uq.edu.au/news/article/2016/11/tiny-einstein-created-super-cold-microscopic-detail|title=Tiny Einstein is created in super-cold microscopic detail|work=UQ News|access-date=2018-10-23|language=en}}</ref> The image is approximately 0.1mm by 0.1mm in size but with a surface 100 million times colder than interstellar space.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gauthier|first1=G.|last2=Lenton|first2=I.|last3=Parry|first3=N. McKay|last4=Baker|first4=M.|last5=Davis|first5=M. J.|last6=Rubinsztein-Dunlop|first6=H.|last7=Neely|first7=T. W.|date=20 October 2016|title=Direct imaging of a digital-micromirror device for configurable microscopic optical potentials|journal=Optica|language=EN|volume=3|issue=10|pages=1136–1143|doi=10.1364/OPTICA.3.001136|issn=2334-2536|arxiv=1605.04928|bibcode=2016Optic...3.1136G|s2cid=118593143}}</ref>

=== Optical Micro-manipulation ===
Rubinsztein-Dunlop's research in laser micro-manipulation involves the use of [[optical tweezers]] to trap objects in three dimensions and exert optical forces onto them. As she explains in her own words, "Optical tweezers act like our normal tweezers, but instead of using mechanical tweezers you are just using laser light that's highly focused: you grab something, and apply force to it to move it. What is beautiful about it is that it's a quantitative method: you can evaluate how far you move an entity and what sort of force you're applying, so you can start interrogating complex biological or solid state systems in a very precise way."<ref name=":6" /> Her group exploits the ability to rotate very small objects using exotic laser modes such as Laguerre Gauss beams, as for example was published in 2014 for a micron size donut shaped rotor.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rubinsztein-Dunlop|first1=Halina|last2=Nieminen|first2=Timo A.|last3=Stilgoe|first3=Alexander B.|last4=Asavei|first4=Theodor|last5=Loke|first5=Vincent L. Y.|date=11 August 2014|title=Driving corrugated donut rotors with Laguerre-Gauss beams|journal=Optics Express|language=EN|volume=22|issue=16|pages=19692–19706|doi=10.1364/OE.22.019692|pmid=25321053|issn=1094-4087|bibcode=2014OExpr..2219692L|s2cid=3471445|doi-access=free}}</ref> In a seminal paper published in 1995 and titled "Direct Observation of Transfer of [[Angular momentum|Angular Momentum]] to Absorptive Particles from a Laser Beam with a Phase Singularity", Rubinsztein-Dunlop's group experimentally showed the spinning of absorptive particles trapped in a singularity beam where the spin direction was controlled based on the sign of the singularity.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=He|first1=H.|last2=Friese|first2=M. E. J.|last3=Heckenberg|first3=N. R.|last4=Rubinsztein-Dunlop|first4=H.|date=31 July 1995|title=Direct Observation of Transfer of Angular Momentum to Absorptive Particles from a Laser Beam with a Phase Singularity|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=75|issue=5|pages=826–829|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.826|pmid=10060128|url=https://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view/UQ:161172/UQ161172.pdf|bibcode=1995PhRvL..75..826H}}</ref>

=== Biophysics ===
Rubinsztein-Dunlop also conducts work in the field of [[biophysics]], notably a study on [[vertigo]] and understanding the body's balance system.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/10/171005102636.htm|title=Vertigo and understanding the body's balance system|work=ScienceDaily|access-date=2018-08-09|language=en}}</ref> At the heart of this research is [[otolith]]s which are little stones in the ears. By manipulating the otoliths in [[zebrafish]] and moving them around, reactions were observed such as how the "fish moves its tail to try to compensate for the interaction with its balance system".<ref name=":6" /> The 2018 UNSW [[Eureka Prizes|Eureka Prize]] for Excellence in Interdisciplinary Scientific Research was awarded to Rubinsztein-Dunlop and the University of Queensland Optical Physics in Neuroscience team based on research using optical trapping and novel microscopes that image how brain circuits function to process motion together with other senses.<ref name=":5" /> She has also conducted research using laser micro-manipulation to examine [[red blood cell]]s to see how long blood can be stored before being used safely; the older the cell, the more likely the [[Elasticity (physics)|elasticity]] changes. Rubinsztein-Dunlop uses optical tweezers to grab the blood cell at both ends and then stretches the cell from one end whilst the other is fixed to measure how much it can stretch.<ref name=":6" />

== Memberships ==
* Rubinsztein-Dunlop is a member of the Scientific Advisory Board of NTT [[Basic research|Basic Research]] Laboratories, Japan.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.brl.ntt.co.jp/E/introduction/advisory.html|title=NTT Basic Research Laboratories|website=www.brl.ntt.co.jp|access-date=2018-08-09}}</ref>
* She is a member of the Editorial Board of the [[Journal of Biophotonics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/18640648/homepage/2475_edbd.html|title=Journal of Biophotonics |website=onlinelibrary.wiley.com|doi=10.1002/(ISSN)1864-0648 |language=en|access-date=2018-08-09}}</ref>
* She is a member of the Advisory Board of the [[Beckman Laser Institute|Beckmann Laser Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bli.uci.edu/newsletter/founder.php|title=Beckman Laser Institute - Founder's Column Arnold Beckman Tribute|website=www.bli.uci.edu|access-date=2018-08-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304193106/http://www.bli.uci.edu/newsletter/founder.php|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*In 2012, Rubinsztein-Dunlop became a Fellow of The Optical Society for pioneering contributions in nano and micro laser manipulation in the fields of optical tweezers and atom optics with applications to biophotonics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/awards_and_grants/fellow_members/recent_fellows/2012_fellows/|title=2012 OSA Fellows|website=|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=17 September 2019}}</ref>
*[[SPIE]] roles: Board of Directors, Diversity and Inclusion Ad Hoc Committee, Fellows Committee, Publications Committee, Strategic Planning Committee, Symposia Committee, Symposium Chair, Conference Program Committee, Conference Chair, Symposium Committee<ref name=":7" />

==Personal life==
She is married to the engineer, Gordon Dunlop.<ref name=":0" />
